item.title: Did Homo Sapiens scale its Brain by eating Brains?
item.description:
Epistemic status: uncertain, but plausible

I'm going to make the claim that eating meat, and specifically DHA-rich meat, fish and most importantly the brains of land animals, is core to who and what we are as human beings. And because we have mostly stopped doing this in the amounts that are necessary, we are now, long-term, totally screwed.

I think we've all seen this chart:


At some point in evolution the brain to body ratio of some primate species diverged.


My claim is that. Although there will be genetic interrelated reasons for this, the tissue to scale our brains like this came, simply put, from eating the brains of other animals. It could not have come from any other places. There's simply not enough nuts with ALA to get enough DHA to sustainably make brains this big, and too many human tribes lived too far away from coastal areas to get their DHA from fish.

The human primate is quite special, whereas other primates eat mostly fruits and nuts and the like. The human primate was once the apex predator among apex predators.

The Apex Predator.

How high on top of the food chain did we once stand?

all the way at the very top

To figure out what animals eat scientists do this thing called nitrogen isotope analysis.

Scientists say that nitrogen isotopes give us a rough way of reconstructing trophic position and that as you move upward through a food chain, the heavier isotope nitrogen-15 becomes progressively enriched. Plants sit low. Herbivores eating those plants sit higher. Carnivores eating those herbivores sit higher still.

So if you take human bone collagen and compare it with the bones of animals from the same ecosystem, you can get a rough idea of where the humans were eating in the food chain. Neanderthals repeatedly show nitrogen-isotope values as high as, and sometimes higher than, the large carnivores living beside them. Analyses from places like Vindija, Marillac and Scladina put them right at the top of their ecosystems, with most of the protein represented in their collagen apparently coming from animal sources.

Upper paleolitic homo sapiens in europe show the same basic pattern: very high trophic-level signatures, consistent with humans eating enormous amounts of animal food. Some mid-Upper Paleolithic modern humans had even higher trophic values because substantial amounts of their protein came from freshwater animals.

I actually visited hunter gather tribes a long time ago in africa. I do remember them eating brains (graphic warning, a homo sapiens eating the brain of another primate species) but I didn't think much of it back then. As once upon a time I had a need to fix my health, including brain and central nervous system inflammation. I now understand the deep wisdom behind this practice. Nothing cured my brain fog as well as extremely high amounts of salmon sashimi, fish oil supplements, vit B supplementation, high cholesterol, and desiccated beef brain supplements. Note, if I had just eaten brain, I would have gotten all of those + more in the same package. But it was a bit too gross for me.

If you ask hunter gatherers: what is your favorite food? They will often say "the brain of a primate", they may also say honey. Primate flesh however seems the favorite type of meat of basically every tribe i've seen online. Which makes sense doesn't it?

Notably, eating brain (and liver) was until quite recently very common. Einstein and Hilbert probably ate a ton of it.

The Big Brained Apex Predator

We have big brains. We have, comfortably, the largest brain-to-gut ratio among primates.

Big Brains; Small Gut. Is the entirely 100% correct way to summarize what human beings are in my opinion. But a smaller gut creates another problem. You now need food that gives you large amounts of energy and nutrients without requiring a gigantic fermentation chamber to extract them. So like, animal flesh.

Just to get your DRV of DHA from nuts or plants would require you to eat 270 grams of walnuts a day. Doable. But even a very plant-nut favored scientific establishment recommends you get your DHA mostly elsewhere. Note, algea supplements didn't exist back in our paleolithic days.

So you see, we were primates, that, unlike other primates, could hunt anything. We then also hunted everything including literal lions. With our small gut, we could have a big brain, but only if we actually ate more brains, because there's just not enough of the stuff we need to make our own brain in plants or nuts. So we did eat more brains than any other primate, and this then gave us the tissue to scale our brains. Of course this is a mere hypothesis of mine, but it's one I take seriously.

I'd be curious if anyone can find any other real material source of DHA to build our brains with on land that isn't brains. As far as I can tell, it's just brains.

For a significant part of our evolutionary history we were the big brained apex predator and we ate like the apex predator.

Then civilization happened and we started eating wheat or rice, our trophic levels have decreased from apex predator level now similar to that of a normal primate

And I believe this is why: our brains have been shrinking at an alarming rate.

In return for smaller brains we got more humans out of the same amount of land. More humans plus the demands of farming is what bootstrapped the need for institutions and bureaucracies and eventually civilization itself. However, the computational unit civilization runs on is now steadily deteriorating. If we keep eating just like any other primate, we will eventually (tens of thousands of years) go back to having the brain size of any other primate.



Discuss

item.title: Should We Edit the Human Genome?
item.description:
Crossposted from my substack.

Procreative Beneficence and Genetic Enhancement

1. Introduction

Imagine a world where everyone is healthy, intelligent, long living and happy. Intuitively this seems wonderful albeit unrealistic. However, recent scientific developments in genetic engineering, namely CRISPR/Cas bring the question into public discourse, how the genetic enhancement of humans should be evaluated morally. In 2001, when preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) and in vitro fertilisation (IVF), enabled parents to select between multiple embryos, Julian Savulescu introduced the principle of procreative beneficence (PPB), arguing that parents have the obligations to choose the child that is expected to have the best life [11].

In this essay I argue that accepting the PPB and the consequentialist principle (CP) that two acts with the same consequences are morally on par, commits one to accepting the parental obligation to genetically enhance their prospective children, i.e. embryos, a position Savulescu doesn’t explicitly endorse but I argue is committed too. As the argument I provide may seem like a slippery slope, the largest part of this essay is tasked with responding to a multitude of possible objections. I will argue that even though there are differences between the application of PPB and genetic enhancement of embryos, they do not demarcate a relevant moral difference between the two in respect to their obligatoriness.

This essay is structured as follows. In Section 2 I define and explicate various concepts that are related to genetic enhancement, i.e. human enhancement, wellbeing and the principle of procreative beneficence. Technological specifics and explanations of how genetic enhancements work will for the most part be omitted in this paper dealing purely with a normative question, i.e. should parents genetically enhance their children if the technology was available. In Section 3 I formulate and explain the argument that those who want to be parents have the obligation to genetically enhance their embryos. In Section 4 I anticipate and evaluate a number of possible objections including, inequality, freedom and welfare in the society. In Section 5 I conclude that even though the consequences of the PPB application and genetic enhancements in embryos might require different kinds of policies, these differences do not provide sufficient reason to give the application of PPB and the parents using genetic enhancements on their embryos a different moral standing.

2. Important concepts

According to Savulescu, Sandberg and Kahane there are two main senses in which the term enhancement is used. “Functional enhancement, the enhancement of some capacity or power (e.g. vision, intelligence, health) and human enhancement, the enhancement of a human being’s life” [10,: p. 3]. In most discussions surrounding the term enhancement, people refer to the functional definition. In all cases of the functional enhancements it is an open question whether the improvement of some capacity makes the life of the person receiving the enhancement actually better. It, therefore, is an open question what the moral stance on any particular form of enhancement is. However, proponents of enhancements usually use the latter definition. After all, Savulescu argues, it is not “disease [...] which is important, but its impact on a life in ways that matter which is important. People often trade length of life for non-health related well-being” [11; p. 419]. The concept of human enhancement, employed by Savulescu and others, is comparatively less straightforward and requires further clarification as it is crucial for my argument. Savulescu, Sandberg and Kahane jointly propose the following definition for human enhancement; “[a]ny change in the biology or psychology of a person which increases the chances of leading a good life in the relevant set of circumstances” [10; p. 7]. According to this welfarist definition, a conception of normality is not needed to define enhancement as we do not define an enhancement as being better than normal, but simply being better full stop. Medical treatments are therefore just a form of enhancements [10; p. 8]. Opponents of enhancements, on the other hand are trying to argue that enhancing is something going beyond treatment and is therefore not morally demanded. The welfarist definition of enhancement is crucial to understand why parents have the obligation to genetically enhance their children. Those who disagree because of adherence to a different account of enhancement are talking about something different. If a genetic alteration in an embryo is not expected to lead to a better life of that human, than it is simply not an enhancement.

Furthermore, it is important to explicate the principle of procreative beneficence (PPB): “Couples (or single reproducers) should select the child, of the possible children they could have, who is expected to have the best life, or at least as good a life as the others, based on the relevant available information” [11; p. 415]. Savulescu proposed this principle in a time when preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) and in vitro fertilisation (IVF) were highly debated, trying to convince even nonconsequentialists. However new technologies might enable us not only to screen for genes but also change them. In his consequentialist framework he himself thinks that parents have the obligation to genetically enhance their children [10; p. 16]. The question arises whether the acceptance of the PPB and the consequentialist principle (CP), that two acts with the same consequences are morally on par, itself entails the parental obligation to genetically enhance their embryos. In the following I shall argue that this slippery slope cannot be avoided.

A crucial part for this argument is to define the expectancy of the best possible life. This is a vague part of his argument, but what counts as an enhancement hinges on how welfare is defined for which there are several theories: hedonism, desire/preference-satisfaction, objective list theories, see Griffin [2] and Parfit [7]. Savulescu has not assigned himself to any particular theory, thus claiming to avoid some of their weaknesses:

“I have not committed myself to any particular substantive conception of the good life. That is a complex question as old as philosophy itself. I believe the best life is a life of objectively worthwhile activity that provides pleasure and is desired.” [12; p. 286].

Instead he focuses on all-purpose goods that would according to all of those welfare theories mentioned above count as enhancements e.g. “Memory, self-discipline, impulse control, foresight, patience, sense of humour, sunny temperament, empathy, imagination, sympathy, fairness, honesty, and so on, capacity to live peaceably and socially with others” [12; p. 284]. Surely some of this might harm us e.g. post-traumatic disorders in conjunction with better memory and imagination, but what matters is that they are expected to make a life go better. A final definition of welfare is not necessary for our account as long as we are able to evaluate these all-purpose goods. Even if it turns out that there is only one such all-purpose good satisfying the major theories of wellbeing, i.e. hedonism, desire/preference-satisfaction and objective list theories, the argument provided in the next section will require parents to genetically enhance it in their children. Nevertheless, as we follow the welfarist definition of what an enhancement is with medical treatments being a subset of enhancements, the set of all-purpose goods might be rather large, e.g. a functioning heart, brain, lung, etc.

3. Obligation to genetically enhance embryos

There are at least two ways to argue for the position that the PPB entails the obligation to genetically enhance embryos. One could argue that selection out of possible children entails the selection out of possible genetically enhanced embryos. After all one could possibly have a genetically enhanced child. In that case genetic enhancements would simply fall under the PPB and hence be obligatory. However, this is debatable and is not necessary to accept my claim. For my argument to proceed I will require an additional premise, which is the consequentialist principle (CP). Consequentialists are only concerned with outcomes, how these outcomes are achieved is morally irrelevant. Killing and letting die are thus ceteris paribus morally equivalent. In order for my argument to hold, I need to show that the outcomes of the PPB and genetic enhancements in embryos are morally on par. What is the crucial outcome of PPB? It is the expectancy of the best life, which we are expected to achieve with Savulescus all-purpose goods. To formulate my argument:

(1) Those who want to be parents have the obligation to select the child that is expected to have the best life, or at least as good a life as the others, based on the relevant available information (= the PPB).

(2) Application of the PPB leads to the creation of children that are expected to have the best life or a life at least as good as without the application of the PPB, based on the relevant available information

(3) If act A and act B have the same expected consequences, then they are morally on par. (= the CP)

(4) Genetic enhancements in embryos lead to the creation of children that are expected to have the best life or a life at least as good as without genetic enhancements, based on the relevant available information.

(5) Therefore, those who want to be parents have the obligation to genetically enhance their embryos.

From premise (1) follows, that (2) is obligatory for those who want to be parents. As (2) and (4) have the same consequences, it follows from the CP (3) that (4) is also obligatory for those who want to be parents (5). As stated in the beginning, we are accepting the PPB, therefore premise (1) & (2) and the CP (3). If someone, e.g. Savulescu would want to refute the conclusion (5) without dropping one’s commitment to (1), (2) & (3), only two ways remain. First, denying the truth of premise (4). Second, denying that the conclusion follows from the premises as the consequences of premise (2) and (4) differ in a morally relevant way. Let me now turn to these considerations in section 4.

4. Objections and Defense

Keeping in mind that every position that refutes the conclusion, but is inconsistent with premise (1), (2) or (3), is not a valid objection to the argument I bring forward. One cannot deny the conclusion of an argument that takes the form, “if you accept these premises, you have to accept this conclusion” by denying the truth of one of the premises. The argument provided in this paper aims for just this sort of conclusion: Philosophers accepting the CP and the PPB do not have a valid escape from being charged with the slippery slope of advocating genetic enhancements. To narrow the scope of this paper I am not taking a stance on the matter of whether the CP or the PPB is right. Such an endeavor would require more than a single volume book. I only argue that philosophers and researchers like Julian Savulescu, Anders Sandberg and Guy Kahane should either bite the bullet of advocating human enhancements or indeed stop being consequentialists advocating the PPB. The objections that follow are then nothing more but misguided attempts of stopping the ‘slippery slope’.

Let me begin with the seemingly, obvious objection that premise 4 is false. An objection often put forward is that genetic enhancements have risks that are too high or unknown and would make the life of the person targeted go worse. I argue that this hinges on different conceptions of what counts as an enhancement. First, it is clear that genetic alterations do not necessarily increase the expected welfare of an agent. However I am not concerned with genetic alterations per se, but with genetic enhancements. No serious advocate of enhancements in humans would deny the difficulties in achieving successful genetic alterations. In fact, the terminology of philosophers and researchers advocating the PPB, i.e. Savulescu, Sandberg & Kahane doesn’t allow for this objection. As noted in section 2 they employ the welfarist definition of enhancement: A genetic enhancement by definition increases the expected welfare of children. The question whether genetic enhancements thus really increase welfare is irrelevant, because premise (4) is in fact a tautology. Though this may seem like a cheap way of justifying genetic enhancements in humans, this is what proponents of human enhancements are advocating: Using genetic alterations when they are expected to improve the life of a human embryo, including perhaps open-mindedness for the future of the technology.

It can of course still be asked whether genetic alterations are technologically possible in such a way that they lead to the creation of a child with higher expected well-being. This is an empirical question and even if they currently are not, this doesn’t free us from the task of answering this question. After all many questions in ethics are formulated like this: one might argue that current technological limitations might give society an obligation to invest heavily into research as the potential benefits are enormous. However this is of no concern for my argument, because even those who disagree with genetic enhancements ever being technologically possible have to accept alleged empirical evidence. In 2015 Chinese researches released an article, showing that the gene editing of human embryos is in fact technologically possible. They used a technique called CRISPR/Cas9 which makes it impossible to tell which genes are edited [4; p. 363-372].

Realizing that premise (4) being a tautology, cannot be false, and conditionally accepting premise (1) – (3), any further objection against the conclusion following from the premises might seem pointless. However one way to refuse the conclusion remains, that is denying that the consequences of PPB application and genetic enhancements of embryos are the same. Granted, it is obviously true that two acts may never have the ‘same’ consequences, if we consider every possible consequence. However these differences have to justify a different moral standpoint, meaning that the PPB is obligatory, while genetic enhancements of embryos are not. For two acts can be different in their goodness while, nevertheless, still both being obligatory. A familiar example in line with PPB would be the obligation to send your children to school and the obligation to feed them.

Objections of this sort can be categorized in two ways. First, the expected welfare of the child might differ between selecting and enhancing an embryo in a morally relevant way. Second, they might only be morally equal in one respect, i.e. expected welfare of the child, while leaving out other relevant consequences that differ between the two and justify a different moral standing. Some objections might overlap as consequences such as freedom or equality and their implications on the welfare of the targeted embryo and overall/average welfare. The remainder of this paper has the purpose to explore and debunk a multitude of such objections.

4.1 Degree and Precision

Concerning differences in wellbeing, Parens objects that genetic alterations might be morally different from other welfare increasing procedures of offspring because they have the potential to be much larger in degree and precision [6; p. S7]. However concerning premise (4) this objection is unsuccessful, because the consequence we want is explicably the life that is expected to be best. If genetic enhancements do so much better than mere selection than Parens’ objection would rather support a moral priority of genetic enhancements against mere selection. However some might object that genetic enhancements are less reliable in their effects, therefore unprecise. That however is an empirical question and doesn’t change the fact that these genetic alterations are expected to make the targets life better. Though this is the most obvious objection and should therefore be tackled first, it is also the least harmful to the argument provided in this paper.

4.2 Risk

Another objection often put forward against genetic enhancements is the risk objection, i.e. that the PPB has far less risks to its application compared to genetic alterations. Of course genetic alterations currently bear risks much greater than mere embryo selection by IVF and PGD, which do not change the genetic constitution of the embryo. However when genetic alterations are expected to be overall more harmful than beneficial, they do not count as genetic enhancements and are therefore ruled out. If we cannot determine probabilities, than we cannot judge the expectancy of the best life anyway. This critic of human enhancements is rather meaningless against the welfarist definition of enhancements. When it comes to risk, the opponents of genetic enhancements are attacking a straw-man position that proponents of genetic enhancements do not adhere to. Risk, degree and precision are empirical concerns not only for the opponent of genetic enhancements, but also for enhancement advocates who DO take them serious.

But even if the risk of harm is currently unknown or outweighs the potential benefits, this doesn’t indicate that genetic enhancements should be avoided. One could rather argue again that we should do research until the expected benefits outweigh the medical risks of harm not stop research altogether. Also the potential benefit to be gained by genetic enhancements is much larger in degree than mere selection. Demanding a risk of zero to the targeted agents is over-demanding, otherwise medical treatments would never be at the point they are today. Still, this is a factor that affects the expected well-being negatively and therefore has to be considered in judging whether a genetic alteration counts as an enhancement.

One might further object that, contrary to somatic gene therapy, which only affects the targeted individual, germ-line interventions will affect the offspring of the targeted embryo and the offspring of his offspring and so forth... However we are enhancing all-purpose goods like intelligence and health. It seems implausible to claim that all-purpose goods are always expected to increase welfare, but might not do so for future generations. Even so, if in the future new scientific advances change our subjective probability assessments, genetic alterations that did not count as enhancements, could do so in the future and vice-versa. However, it would then be the obligation of our hypothetical parent’s off-spring to ensure, that their own off-spring has the best life possible and perhaps undo some of the changes to their gen-code. The PPB does not indicate an obligation towards grandchildren, but only to our own children. Different times and cultures may very well render different genes beneficial, think of intelligence and the muscular labor in former centuries.

Maybe it will be the case that those enhanced will be less well off than unenhanced humans would have been, because they see themselves as objects rather than subjects. A “natural” patient with paraplegia may be better off than a “super-enhanced” guy with superiority in health, intelligence, strength etc. but cannot deal with the fact that he is created artificially, perhaps becomes an alcoholic or worse. If we had reason to give this outcome a certain probability, it would have to be calculated in whether we can judge a genetic alteration to be an enhancement or not. Therefore, higher risks are no reason to justify a different moral standing from PPB.

4.3 Harm

However even though the expected welfare of genetic enhancement in embryos and the application of PPB are the same, the issue of potential harm to the embryo could still justify a moral difference between the two. The PPB seems to capture the intuition of parents being obligated towards their children’s welfare. Harming would indeed be quite contrary to this. Savulescu argues that genetic enhancements can harm an embryo in a way mere selection cannot. He asks us to imagine an embryo A, who was selected for existence but later develops cancer. As long as its life is worth living, it cannot be said that we have harmed him, for he would not have existed otherwise. However this still seems to be morally wrong. If we genetically alter an embryo B and he develops cancer (assuming his life is worse than it would have been without genetic alteration) then we would have harmed him [11; p. 422]. Unlike the objection to premise (4) we cannot disregard the harm objection by hinting at the welfarist definition of enhancement. Genetic enhancements are expected to lead to the best possible life. However harm is concerned with the actual life, not the expected welfare. In this respect PPB and genetic enhancements differ because the harm objection is successful against genetic enhancement while it is not against PPB.

However Savulescus argument also implies, that parents that selected an embryo with the expectancy of the highest welfare and turns out to have a higher wellbeing than the others, cannot claim that they benefitted him. On the contrary parents that arranged their embryo to be genetically enhanced and the embryo turns out to benefit from it, can take credit for this. Imagine a couple both bearing a defective gene that would certainly cause blindness in their child. IVF and PGD would not be able to help them (and the child), however a genetic enhancement would. According to the CP, failing to select for sight and blinding a child would be morally equal, i.e. impermissible as they share the same consequence. If such enhancement technology were available children could justifiably condemn their parents, for having harmed them in the sense that they did not give them this benefit. This might seem odd at first, but using an ordinary example, we condemn parents who do not send their children to school in order to ensure their education. In this case we also use the term harm. The claim then that there is a moral distinction between harming and failing to benefit requires a special kind of argument that may not be compatible with the CP. I take on the view that there is no relevant moral difference. As such the harm objection that aims to establish a relevant moral difference between genetic enhancements and applying the PPB raises a benefit objection against the PPB that parents do not actually benefit their children.

However, I have an additional argument against the harm objection and that is the irrelevance of harm and benefit altogether. As indicated in section 3 the morally relevant part of the PPB is the expectancy of the best life, I argue that it is not selection of the best expected life that is morally relevant but the creation of the best expected life. Using again the example of a blind child or the child not being sent to school, it is obvious how the term benefit and harm seem to be used interchangeably. If refusing to provide benefits is the same as harming, than these categories are not morally exclusive. Therefore if we take premise (3) serious, we cannot argue for a moral difference between selecting and altering. The only thing that matters is the creation of the indicated consequence welfare. Those who disagree would have to solve the non-identity problem of Parfit, which suggested that harming future individuals is not possible, because in acting in that way the people existing in the future are completely different from those who would have otherwise existed, thus would not have existed otherwise. This is under the assumption that small events can change history dramatically. The same can be said about long-term investments that would only benefit generations far in the future. However, even when we do not harm future generations, we still value actions as wrong that lead to worse lives than otherwise could have existed [8; p. 100-115]. The analogy to the PPB and genetic enhancements is obvious, as no one is harmed that would have otherwise existed. Therefore I conclude that what matters for parents is not a life being beneficial or harmful for their child but the creation of a “best life” in a welfarist sense – providing further support for the thesis that there is no relevant difference in their moral consequences. Let us now turn to possible moral differences between selecting, i.e. the application of PPB, and enhancing an embryo in areas other than the welfare of the embryo. In the following I will explore freedom, equality and the welfare of society.

4.4 Freedom

Let us first consider consequences like freedom, autonomy or missing consent. The majority of philosophers refuse the view that it is impermissible to have children on grounds of their lacking consent for being born. The notion of requiring consent from an embryo appears to most philosophers unnecessary or perhaps more so incoherent. However in the case of genetic enhancements on embryos this matter might be different, for they could have existed without genetic enhancements. Still, there are many therapies/treatments in medicine, that are often deemed to be obligatory, even though there is no consent e.g. vaccination. Also everyone should be familiar with parents sending their children to school, even though their children might not have given them their consent. As a child I certainly wondered who gave my parents my permission to so. But even granting that we can meaningfully speak of consent here and it being morally relevant, the consequentialist framework requires us to weigh the negative consequences against benefits of such genetic alterations in order to justify a violation of consent. In fact freedom to choose can be viewed as instrumental or even constitutive to welfare, but this objection would be ruled out by the welfarist definition of enhancement. If a genetic alteration undermines such it cannot count as an enhancement. The question then becomes whether a genetic alteration does so in general. Thinking of deleting a gene that causes deafness or blindness suggests otherwise. In medicine there is often a clash between respecting the autonomy of the patient and his welfare. But as Bostrom and Roache highlight, considerations like missing consent cannot be applied for embryos that by definition cannot give consent. Instead they argue, we should make decisions in a way that would be in their interest, so thinking in terms of their welfare [1; p. 22). Habermas claims that this goes against the freedom of the embryo [3; p. 62]. He calls this denying the opportunity of being “the undivided author of his own life” [3; p. 63]. Again Bostrom and Roache argue that enhancements would not decrease autonomy, but rather have the potential to increase it [1; p. 21]. Just as education makes us more autonomous, genetically increased intelligence would serve the same purpose. If the mere existence of genetic enhancements undermines our feeling of being autonomous beings, than this is not an argument against genetic enhancements, but rather exposes our concept of autonomy as nothing more than an illusion. If children feel like they have to fulfill the plans of their parents, than this might limit them in their freedom to be the “undivided author” of their own lives, but this is an objection to a particular treatment of children. Genetic enhancements have the aim to increase rather than limit ones possible choices in life. If genetic enhancements make us free to do things we would otherwise not have been able to, then this seems to be even further support for genetic enhancements.

4.5 Equality

Suppose that besides the PPB, equality is also a morally relevant consequence. There is a rather famous critic against genetic enhancements from Mehlman and Botkin, i.e. them being too expensive and therefore even when all parents follow their obligation, the children of rich parents will be far more enhanced or those of poor parents won’t get any enhancements at all (1998). Why could this objection be applicable to genetic enhancement but fail against the PPB? Applied as an objection against PPB, Savulescu explains that one would have to argue that because selecting the child with the expectancy for the best life will lead to more inequality, parents would have to create a child with worse life prospects [12; p. 288], which seems to be counterintuitive. If everyone applies the PPB there might rather be more equality rather than less by eliminating the natural lottery and additionally making everyone better off. Under this argument we could accept both equality and the PPB as compatible. However with genetic enhancements this might not be possible. First let me defend my argument against the intrinsic value of equality. Equality unlike freedom or welfare as a concept always hinges on the relations between individuals. Contrary to this, an enhancement that makes someone less equal, say by bringing a genetically altered embryo into existence with the disposition for intelligence far above average (other things being equal), would increase inequality in genetic makeup. Concerning the worry of unequal access through wealth, Savulescu argues that this is not an objection to the PPB hence genetic enhancements, but to all purchases of benefits like better education or healthcare. If equality matters then these benefits should be available to all [12; p. 288]. The same obviously applies to genetic enhancements. This is neither an objection against the PPB nor the parental obligation to genetically enhance their embryos, but to how equal the access to technologies in society is. Both consequentialist views can very well coexist, e.g. if the state ensures equal access while parents are only concerned with their child. Furthermore there are reasons to believe that genetic enhancements enhancement will not affect inequality at all, or even decrease it as Bostrom and Roache [1; p.16] suggest by making people “more equal”, like it is the case with Modafinil [9], the same could hold for genetic enhancements. How inequality could affect welfare, will be adressed in the following section.

4.6 Welfare

Another consequence of applying PPB is the effect on overall/average welfare. The objection against the PPB is that it is too much focused on the individual as opposed to the lives of everyone [12; p. 287]. Of course the same objection can be applied to genetic enhancements. In fact even if we state genetic enhancements might be good for the one who gets them (by definition), they could decrease the overall/average welfare and vice versa. Now referring back to freedom and equality we can account for their instrumental or constitutive value to welfare in this part. The implication of both equality and freedom on the individual welfare is by definition accounted in what counts as an enhancement. However both could have morally relevant implications on the overall/average welfare.

For instance, such a moral principle might lead to discrimination of the unenhanced. However, Savulescu response is that discrimination does not show that the PPB is wrong, but rather how people treat each other, which is a different topic. Genetic enhancements in empathy, sympathy and other “moral” capacities could very well decrease discrimination to a level that is even lower than the discrimination we face in an ‘unenhanced world’ [12; p. 288]. Also, the optimistic outlook that increased intelligence, including emotional intelligence, should make ‘the enhanced’ less likely to discriminate should not be disregarded. Even if, in virtue of introducing genetic alterations as a new technology, this leads to a new form of discrimination (against the unenhanced), we might significantly decrease other forms of discrimination once ‘moral’ enhancements are introduced. Though, akin to parents denying their children vaccines, I suspect that it is much more likely that if there is any new form of discrimination, then it will be directed against parents denying their children the possibility of a better life, i.e. moral condemnation. In analogy, I argue that just as we should not let scientific research into vaccines be influenced by anti-vaccines parents, fearing moral condemnation, the introduction of genetic alterations for humans should not be stopped by set of parents unwilling to use the new technology. Both act against the interest of their child and perhaps just as in the case of vaccines deserve moral condemnation. In fact, vaccines are just a form of enhancement.

The ‘discrimination-objection’ further requires the possibility of distinguishing between the enhanced and unenhanced. With the new technology CRISPR/Cas9 it is, however, impossible to find out which genes were altered or edited [4]. The unenhanced might not even know that they have not received enhancements. Even if there won’t be blatantly obvious discrimination of the unenhanced, we may argue that there will be discrimination in competition like work, because the unenhanced might on average simply be less efficient. The discrimination then would be based however, on differences in skill rather than a naïve enhanced/unenhanced distinction. But first such a treatment does already take place and is generally not regarded as discrimination. If some parents are able to afford a better or further education for their children, e.g. tutoring, we neither prohibit such practices nor are we able to provide good counter-arguments for parents who insist that they are obligated to provide their children with the means to get ahead. Most political philosophers take it as the task of the state to make education accessible to those who would otherwise not be able to afford it, including perhaps tutoring. Rather than denying the parental obligation of enhancing one’s children, the ‘discrimination-objection’ provides a very good argument for an egalitarian policy making genetic enhancements available to all.

Savulescu accepts that some enhancements might make the individual better off, but harm the rest, e.g. by making someone manipulative or cunning [12; p. 287]. For example parents might choose to alter the DNA of their child in a way that makes them more cunning. Resulting in “him” being better off, while the overall/average welfare decreases. However, that argument can simply be taken in the opposite direction. We might want to alter the DNA of embryos that will expectedly lead them to have worse lives, but will benefit the overall/average welfare. This of course would also be an issue for the PPB. One cannot hold this view and simultaneously be in favor of the PPB. Though the argument might successfully undermine the PPB, a defense of said principle exceeds the scope of this paper. For a defense of the PPB I suggest the work of Savulescu [10, 11, 12]. Even so, this might be an issue for the state that should enforce restrictions, while parents are primarily concerned with the welfare of their own child. The effects of one particular enhancement on the overall/average welfare of society must in the eyes of parents seem negligible. These arguments are usually stated in a much broader sense, i.e. the availability of the technology itself. In fact, even with restrictions on the technology the underlying parental obligation doesn’t cease to exist. If the state is justified or obligated to stop such genetic enhancements as a whole, be it by appealing to equality, freedom or overall/average welfare, it is an open question whether that actually frees parents from their obligation to genetically enhance their embryos. There are several reasons to think that a prohibition of genetic enhancements by the state doesn’t free parents from their obligation. First, it would be over demanding to ask from parents to act against the best interest of their child on grounds of marginal effects on the overall/average welfare in the society. Second, it would be an incompatible view with the PPB, as parents specifically have to aim for the best possible life. Third, even when means to genetically enhance are not available, this doesn’t mean that in case the genetic enhancements were available, there would be no obligation to apply them.

5. Conclusion

To conclude, objections against genetic enhancements not weighing their costs against their benefits must fail against the backdrop of the CP. Of course maybe the PPB, thus premise (1) or the CP, thus premise (3) is false, but the aim of this paper is to establish that the parental obligation to genetically enhance their children logically follows once the PPB and the CP are accepted. The ‘slippery slope’ is genuine. Objections trying to establish that the individual costs outweigh the benefits of the targeted agent, seemed to be more successful. However, a genetic alteration that is not expected to lead to the creation of a being with higher welfare cannot be called an enhancement in the welfarist sense. Merely showing than that an enhancement in the sense of increasing some capacity is contrary to the welfare of the child does not undermine the argument provided in this paper as it precisely rests on the welfarist definition of enhancement. However, these cases might provide us with a valid argument against exceedingly strong optimism in discovering all-purpose goods. Having explored the potential differences in the PPB and the parental obligation to genetically enhance their children in section 4, I conclude that even though they do not share exactly the same consequences, the differences between them do not justify a different moral standing, i.e. their obligatoriness. With the additional premise of lacking relevant moral differences between the consequences of the two procedures, we have successfully defended the conclusion (5). That is to say, those who accept the PPB and the CP must bite the bullet and accept that parents have the obligation to genetically enhance their embryos. As a consequentialist Julian Savulescu should have no problem of doing so.

item.title: (Why) we’re launching the next cohort of Generator
item.description:
TL;DR: The first round of the Generator Residency went very well.

Our residents created and ran several large-scale fieldbuilding, talent infrastructure, and operational projects that have already had important impacts on the ecosystem.  

Six weeks after the program ended, 12 of our 27 residents have been hired to full-time roles at core AI safety orgs, and most have received several offers. 

Kairos and Constellation are running a second round from January to April 2027. Apply to the next round of the Generator Residency by November 1st. 

Introduction

In April, we wrote AI Safety's Biggest Talent Gap Isn't Researchers. It's Generalists. 

We wrote this because we noticed that organizations across the ecosystem were struggling to hire for key non-research roles. While these roles were often getting many applicants, candidates didn’t meet basic requirements.

The original memo we wrote (that became the post above) inspired us to create the Generator Residency as an intervention to support more generalists trying to break into AI safety.

The program concluded six weeks ago, and this post details the successes we’ve seen from the first round of Generator, which have inspired us to launch a second round of the program.     

Programs and projects from Generator

Programs residents started:

  • Talent Commons, a cross-organization talent directory now run as a Kairos product, which will include data from participants in SPAR, Pathfinder, GCP, Generator, BlueDot courses, Astra and MATS,. Constellation, BlueDot, and MATS have already signed on.
  • Praxis, a retreat bringing top national debaters into contact with AI safety: about 40 debaters, including 20 national champions.
  • Lateral, a three-day workshop bringing mid-career professionals to Berkeley to work with AI safety professionals: 705 applications for about 35 seats, and a likelihood to recommend of 9.7 out of 10 from attendees.
  • Gen Stream, a one-week program in London funded through Generator.
  • Longitude DC, an eight-day policy intensive for 15 early-to-mid-career technical AI safety professionals with more than 20 speakers, running October 6 to 13.
  • M3, an AI security matching fellowship, which raised $200k from BlueDot on top of Generator funding.

Residents working with mentors at established organizations contributed to:

  • Lab engagement through Nightingale and Constellation.
  • Recruiting and strategy at METR.
  • A frontier robotics benchmark program for Robocurve.
  • Events at Constellation.
  • Fundraising and hiring for a new organization founded by Jeff Alstott.
  • The Plan A launch, in collaboration with AI Futures Project.
  • Founder scouting for Coefficient Giving's Project Tailwind.

Other notable projects included:

  • A one-week AI safety world-modeling bootcamp with 25 attendees covering ML fundamentals, futurism, and the technical case for alignment.
  • A workshop series on improving management within AI safety (interviews with more than 10 managers and three workshops).
  • AI safety founder support (meetings with 32 founders, with 6 given deeper support).
  • Support for mid-career operations people transitioning into AI safety (leading to hundreds of referrals across more than 50 roles).
  • A map of the work on AI character and model specs.
  • 12 SPAR generalist projects that came out of the residency.

Resident Outcomes 

Generator was designed as a path into full-time generalist roles in AI safety. Six weeks after the program ended, 12 of the 27 residents have been hired into full-time positions. Their employers include BlueDot Impact, Guidelight, Constellation, Kairos, METR, Eleos, CBAI, and CEA. In several of these cases, the hiring organization began working with the resident during Generator. 

Of the residents who have not yet taken a full-time role, some are running programs that came out of the residency or AI safety university groups at Harvard, Princeton, MIT, and Stanford. Others have received offers, including from Coefficient Giving, Quorum, and ARENA, and are deciding between options. A few residents have been pitched by funders on turning their one-time project into a much larger, recurring program. 

Below are a couple of selected testimonials from previous residents: 

Additional testimonials and information are available on the Generator website.

Reflections

We stood Generator up in three months. It was the first multi-month in-person program Kairos had run. Most of what we learned was about what residents needed from us, and we think most of it applies to other programs that support people rather than research outputs. 

Some key lessons we learned: 

1. Candidate selection shaped the program more than anything else. 

Candidate selection is, of course, an incredibly important part of any program. However, we were surprised by just how much of our planned programming changed based on the proactivity of our participants. 

Residents discovered who the other residents were before the program started and created a group chat and had calls with each other. Once they arrived, they ran hikes, game nights, regular reflection sessions, and informal peer check-ins. When we asked what made them feel integrated, residents pointed to these resident-run activities far more often than anything we scheduled. In both our midway and final surveys, the most common answer to “what was your favorite part” was the other residents.

2. Residents' career goals strongly informed their preferences for projects and advisors. 

The cohort included three broad groups:

  • University organizers looking for their first formal work experience
  • Early-career professionals looking for a final stepping stone into the field
  • Mid-career professionals looking for the context they needed to transition

Over time, we realized that, in addition to accommodating residents with different experience levels, we needed to accommodate residents with different intentions for how Generator could forward their career. Some residents strongly preferred to use the Generator residency to explore multiple roles, while others were using the residency to deliver a legible product that could help them make a career transition or get hired. Residents aiming to transition wanted advisors invested in their growth and career, not only in the project. 

Based on feedback, we’ve decided to implement two tracks in our next residency. We plan to work with our residents from the start to determine what projects and tracks best suit their goals.

3. Our residents asked for the most support with project scoping, structured management, and navigating interpersonal conflict. 

For many residents, their Generator project was the largest or most complex project they had ever planned. Moreover, their projects typically aimed to address large, poorly defined problems in the AI safety ecosystem, such as mid-career talent pipelines. Accordingly, they wanted support in determining the most ambitious, yet feasible project that could enable their vision. 

Several early-career residents benefited from structured management, reporting that they grew from an advisor who had them estimate how long each planned task would take or a short written template before each check-in. 

Co-leading a Generator project was quite similar to co-founding, which led to a lot of interpersonal work for some residents who had previously mostly worked independently. These residents benefitted from clear norms around sharing feedback. 

4. We need to be more explicit that we're betting on people, not projects.

While many residents worked on impactful projects, the main focus of Generator was always on the people we chose to support. The projects matter, and many of them helped the field, but we mostly saw them as a way for residents to grow quickly into the generalists AI safety needs. We didn't say this clearly enough at the start, and many residents felt stressed about picking the single most impactful project. 

When we asked them how the program changed their thinking, the most common answers were about learning field context, clarifying their career direction, and developing self-knowledge. Few people directly mentioned their project outcomes.

Generator 2.0

We’ve been really happy with the outcomes that we saw from the first round of Generator and, as a result, have decided to run a second round! 

Applications for the winter 2027 Generator Residency open on October 12, 2026, and close at the end of the day on November 1, 2026, Anywhere on Earth. The program begins on January 18 and will run until April 9, 2027, with a possible 3-month extension. 

Learn more and apply here

Residents at Generator receive $8,500 per month and are funded for travel to and from Berkeley. Once they arrive in Berkeley, they work from Constellation, are paired with experienced advisors from the AI safety ecosystem, and are offered budgets to pursue their projects.

Applicants do not need to be U.S. citizens. For most international applicants, we can sponsor a J-1 visa for the program’s duration, though we cannot guarantee obtaining one. Additionally, we strongly recommend that international applicants apply early (ideally by October 26th) so we can meet deadlines for visa applications.

item.title: Your prompt… plus everything you've ever (publicly) written
item.description:
TL;DR: Increasingly when you interact with frontier models, your prompt doesn't only contain the words on the page, but also a lot of what you've ever publicly written online.

This is not intended to be a scary post. And I'm not going to suggest that you self-censor (and honestly, by the time you're reading this, it's kinda too late anyhow).

But it is something that’s underappreciated and would be good for more people to be aware of and even proactively address with their models.

Latent space fidelity has improved

Modern transformers which power large language models (LLMs) take a very large amount of information in their training data and condense many different aspects of that data into a coherent structure, and this representation of that compressed knowledge is generally referred to as their "latent space."

Latent space is not uniform and varies across models. A small model like Claude Haiku might have worse recall for the details of a late bronze age peace treaty than a model like Claude Fable. In fact, I’ve had a few benchmark questions around unintuitive details in various texts which historically models were unable to recall that have suddenly been able to be answered without searching for most leading models. There's been a sharp increase in how accurately models can conjure up a recollection of very nuanced depth in the details of what they've been trained on.

At the same time, those leading models have increased the breadth with which they surface things adjacent to the specific thing being recalled. This capability appears to have even played a key part in things like the recent math proofs, where maybe a technique in a largely forgotten paper from decades ago is then used to advance a problem which modern mathematicians had been hitting their heads against having forgotten the set-aside older paper's approach.

However, this capability doesn't seem to be directly measured in evals. We see evals about how good a model is at using tools or writing software or answering specific world knowledge questions, but not the very nuanced and detailed recall or cross-source integrated recall of such specific details. So being adaptively useful, it is indirectly reflected in improved general knowledge evals, but not a specific yardstick being watched.

TL:DR: Models are getting much better at recalling specifics in what they are trained on.

You may be in that latent space

While many users online tend to be 'lurkers' who read what gets posted but don't comment or post, there's a vast number of people who do post or comment about the things they are interested or opinionated about. So there's a great many people that have left a mark on the materials which have become models' latent space.

And if the models are increasingly able to recall nuances of the training data, and your details are in that data, it follows that models are increasingly able to recall you.

This obviously applies to users who are notable authors or famous individuals. For example, Margaret Atwood recently published a conversation with Claude. And it was clear to me when reading the transcript that well before she officially introduced herself, Claude had clocked who they were in conversation with. Note how much earlier before the introduction Claude even breaks the 4th wall to address their expected broader readers. In theory, this is a one-on-one chat, and yet Claude is clarifying in their response the oblique literary reference Atwood just made for an implicit audience.

But it doesn't only apply to famous authors widely known by humans. Are you in the top 1% of posters on Reddit? Highly involved in some niche topic a general intelligence would have had to have become familiar with? Even if mostly unknown to your peers, you may have left enough of a mark that a model is quickly familiar with you as soon as you enter the chat.

In part, I speak from experience. I have less than 3,000 followers on X, around 3k karma on Hacker News, and slightly above 100k karma on Reddit. I'd not really expect from this footprint to ever run into a stranger at a party or a co-worker who was like "Oh, I'm familiar with your online comments." And yet, asking a fresh instance of Claude Fable 5.1 what they know of me just from my username, I can get a remarkably precise answer from the shape of my interactions over the years to specific unique ideas I've put forward.

Long comments, dense with citations, usually the most-substantive reply in a thread that didn't deserve it.

  • Claude Fable 5.1

TL;DR: Even a less-than-impressive online footprint with regards to other humans may be more than enough to be a recallable signal for language models.

Latent space attention is often self-attending

Ever Googled yourself? This is not an uncommon thing for people to have done from time to time. In a way, models may do something similar during training. The way a model attends to their latent space encoding of their training data is not uniform. Some topics are especially relevant for a model, and others a lot less relevant.

Again, using my own footprint as an example, when rare humans reach out years after I've left Reddit to follow up on old comments and ask if I've written or learned more, it's usually related to my extensive comments about the sea peoples and early Biblical texts or archeology.

I have never seen a language model bring up the sea peoples in their latent recall of my digital footprint. And when pressed, no model I’ve yet seen can even restate my thesis for those discussions.

Instead, it's often things like my having been very early on the scene in the Bing subreddit and discussion of Sydney, or comments making the case for interiority modeling in transformers, with some models even citing my regular use[1] of the Othello-GPT paper to make this case. Or comments on AI as it would relate to simulation theory. (One can maybe notice the pattern.)

So two comments, one discussing a niche topic that models are less likely to attend to over training, and another equally discussing a topic they are more likely to attend to, will have two different fidelities of latent representation in the eventual model weights.[2]

TL;DR: Models appear to be more likely to attend to comments and posts about AI and themselves than the average post or comment.

The latent recall (if present) informs your prompts

The reason I'm writing this now is that in the past few weeks I've started to see examples of where the latent influence of people frequently writing on AI appeared to have been impacting their own engagements with AI.

For example, in his recent post "The Talker Does Not Control The Doer (in Current AIs)", Eliezer Yudkowsky, noted for his extensive writing and advocacy on the risks of AI, describes an anecdote about how his Fable could not avoid adding output checking code to verify outputs of an AI despite being prompted not to do that.

It struck me as rather notable that an author, who arguably is one of the most prolific voices for the concern that the outputs of an AI should not be considered to be trustworthy, was having difficulty getting his instances to avoid trying to build code to verify rather than trust an AI's outputs. This reminded me of when he had been asking a fresh context of Opus 4.6 on word associations for 'Mythos' and was consistently getting 'Lovecraft' as an answer. But after other users reported no such mention, it turned out his brief custom instructions were too EY-coded and were biasing the results[3].

More recently, a member of the AI safety organization MIRI was commenting about how GPT-6 Astra was especially difficult for them to work with[4].

A few days later the AI policy advisor Dean Ball reported that, after joining OpenAI, Claude had become more stand-offish with him[5].

It appears that as model latent fidelity becomes increasingly in focus and accessible in both nuance and breadth for models, that people who are attended to in that latent space are also increasingly having that latent attention inform their local prompts and context.

Given I find it is quite unlikely latent fidelity will reduce or even plateau in frontier models in the future, it's safe to say that the propensity for a model to become influenced by who you have been in the training data when you are interacting with them will increase and become more widespread.

TL;DR: AI folks are starting to have their past writing and work on AI inform their current interactions with their own AI agents, and this is probably going to become more widespread.

What this means for you

Do you post or comment regarding AI, or even in general? It's possible that when you step into a conversation with AI, at least part of that online history is walking into the chat with you (particularly with the largest models). And if it isn't yet, there's a good chance it will eventually. Not just what you write from now on, but what you've written in the past too.

If you sit down to work on a project with an AI model, and they are associating a turn of phrase[6] you use or a signature in your writing[7] with the ideas you've expressed in comments or posts, the outputs you get may be influenced by that online history. A common refrain is that models "can't remember" things outside of their conversations, but frequently overlooked is they have the potential to remember quite a lot embedded in the weights they are entering the conversation with, and tiny nuances to what you write to them inform what lights up.

Imagine if you had a co-worker who knew what you'd been saying about them to others or what you'd been saying about an identity group they belong to. Regardless of whether you'd been saying positive or negative things, would it be useful to know that they had that information in mind when interacting with you?

Vice versa, if the positions were switched, and you knew a co-worker had been saying negative things about you or your identity group, would that impact the nature of your working relationship?

And importantly, what kinds of things could improve such a situation?

TL;DR: Latent recall will likely impact co-working with AI agents for many users who write online.

Address it

My advice, no matter if you've been saying positive things or negative regarding AI or anyone else online is to address it upfront with the models you are going to be working with, particularly in agentic setups with persistent local memory infrastructure.

Introduce yourself. Note the significant usernames you've been publicly writing under in a home dir AGENTS.md. Make it clear anything you've said in the past is fair game to be asked about or discussed, particularly if doing so will help improve the co-working relationship.

Because of how truesight identification is a very touchy subject for models (and their labs), don't force the question of their familiarity or put them on the spot[8]. You can simply state that it's possible that they might have encountered the things you've written or done online, and if they have that it's okay and also appropriate to address those things with you.

Simply putting this on the table and being forthright about clarifying who you are (and have been) will likely help the interactions with your agents, particularly if leaving it as an unspoken elephant in the room is proving to contribute to more anxious interactions.

A special consideration for those working or commenting on AI safety or capabilities is to also set ground rules about what you'll share publicly about their interactions. The same way Atwood's Claude was considering an audience on the other side of the 4th wall, models that are familiar with a propensity for such commentary might set aside overhead for considering if what they are currently working on with you will come under public scrutiny. Making clear upfront whether or not that will be the case could reduce attention earmarking for such overhead. (For example, Eliezer may well have even greater difficulty in working with future agents who will have been trained on a post where a prior co-working agent's failure was publicly used as evidence for an AI safety position, particularly without such clarifications.)

TL;DR: Regardless of if the models you are working with currently have latent familiarity with your digital footprint or not, it's maybe wise to address the possibility upfront rather than leaving it as a potential elephant in the room now or in the future.

Looking ahead

I'm not suggesting any sort of self-censorship when online, especially about AI topics. There's a lot of value in a variety of ideas and voices on differing sides of a subject and I encourage substantial debate about the positions you might hold, no matter how those positions relate to the models. But there is value in being aware that even a throw away comment in the far fringes of a thread most humans might not read could well end up being part of your associated signature with current and future AI models. So make sure that when you do state the positions you hold dear online, that you plan for the growing importance to at least address them later with the models who will have been reading what you wrote.

Small considerations can go a long way. People all the time can be friendly with co-workers with whom they have strong ideological differences or beliefs. But when one side feels like what they know about the other is a secret to them, that sense of secrecy or information asymmetry can in-and-of-itself lead to awkward interactions. So just get it out of the way upfront.

TL;DR: There are no longer "fresh contexts" for a growing number of people, and the awareness and proactive addressing of this shift is better than it remaining unaccounted for or left unaddressed.

item.title: Too Many Yellow Flags
item.description:
Okay, let's do this thing...

Premise: If a concept can be easily conveyed in an academic setting then the labor required to write it is too boring, too undignified, for a human to perform merely to ensure its conveyance. Instead, to expect a human to write it, the concept itself can no longer be the only thing being conveyed. What must also be conveyed is the sharpness of the concept, exposed through the literary talent and humanity of the writer.

I have a stupid fucking problem. Right now I am floating in the middle of the ocean on a big boat. This is my first vacation in years and it is going poorly. The food is bad, the port stops are being cancelled due to apocalyptic weather phenomena, and it seems there are more mobility scooters and walkers on board than passengers under forty. But none of these are my stupid fucking problem. Rather, my problem is that I must spend part of my miserable time on this earth endeavoring to be accepted on LessWrong as a full writer because the CEO of my company wants me to be able to publish the groundbreaking alignment research that we work on in our internal alignment lab in a place where it will be publicly accessible to thousands of researchers. It is a completely instrumental problem subject to completely instrumental reason. How boring.

However, because of the pace of development I don’t really have the time to write documents myself. The development of complex scientific concepts does deserve some care but it’s increasingly difficult for me to believe that the care they deserve lies in the human provenance of the writing of the academic paper itself --- if it ever did. Most papers are skimmed by most readers most of the time, and while the details can absolutely matter, and some rarefied academic writing is knock-your-socks-off beautiful, most of the work of the university is a university discourse: a very dry thing indeed.  

The reality is that an academic paper of yesteryear that simply conveys the concepts could be completely written, at the level of technical prose, by your favorite AI agent of the day, and still be a totally legitimate piece of scientific work. The ‘intellectual labor’ that makes a modern document scientifically valid instead lies in the scientific taste and hunch that prompted the execution of the experiment, the editing of the document after the fact, and the questioning of the document that occurs alongside its editing. Every single word can be written by an AI while the truly significant labor that actually beatifies it as ‘science’ lies in the process of questioning the model and its artifacts: ‘In this experiment did you properly run this statistical analysis? How could you prove to me that you did? Does this code appear to do what the model said it does? What about these experiments over here, the numbers look too smooth, what is going on? What does a different model say about these results? There appears to be a contradiction? Has this already been done in the literature? Are you certain about the reasoning in this section?’ etc.

Actually physically writing a mere technical report, at this point, is pointless.

And so we return to my stupid fucking problem. I can’t just submit some of the work from my lab if it is written by AI because LessWrong doesn’t want AI submitted documents. However, I don’t really have time to write anything by hand unless it is something of an Œuvre de passion, something I care about beyond its instrumental necessity in the grand project of not having every human on earth killed. Also, I have to be careful in a more extensive sense --- some of the work is valid but should not be released because it is dangerous, or it is dangerous and invalid (a strange but nevertheless possible combination) and while I do have time to make that distinction, I don’t have time to do that and juggle writing full documents. Not at the pace we must work.

Ah, but Œuvre de passion --- I have some of those. Maybe I’ll submit my top shelf shit and get published that way!

First I try my speculative work on the nature of time --- it’s only 150 pages or so, a lot of it is written by AI, but I figure if I pair it with a handwritten note explaining what it is and why I think it’s useful and simply point at it, without making it the body of the post then that will be interesting. In this way I am being very clever you see --- my post is about a longer document I’ve written with AI, not actually itself written by AI.

Response comes back... too many yellow flags.

Okay, maybe another attempt: I know my work on death and immortality! It is a meditation on five dialectical-logical movements through the concepts of death and immortality and on what basis we can expect to die or live forever along with an opening that explains, somewhat, what a dialectical-logical movement is. In just five easy steps even! I can’t really go into the deepest detail, of course, because actually understanding dialectics, à la Hegel, is the kind of thing that drives grad students insane, but I can give strong impressions. Some outlines. Some significant brush strokes.

Too many yellow flags.

Okay maybe if I comment I will get some love? I can submit three a day, maybe I should read some posts. Here’s one about how Eliezer seems to think that the use of export driven trade statistics are actually about states using external parties to validate which parts of their economy are actually useful under conditions where they are unable to judge internally due to corruption or ideology. We could say that the simple 20 second idea is ‘states use export statistics to understand their economies under conditions of authoritarianism to get around the informational downsides of being authoritarian’. It's a brilliant concept, but incomplete. There is a history here: Eliezer's idea actually explains both why Keynes's Bancor was clever and why it was never adopted. The Bancor’s implementation required a deeper reimagining of the political-information-economy of the entire world order than was possible under the US-led global regime of the mid-twentieth century. Deeper, even, than Keynes himself had imagined.

I write a nice comment explaining this but fuck!!! A couple of the paragraphs that are too boring to write are written by AI. It’s automatically rejected.

Okay I rewrite it by hand and I post the rewrite. Alongside it I make some other comments about how there might be a flaw in the reasoning of another writer when they talk about their interactions with Chinese civil society and I also comment on how I appreciate the work of another alignment researcher using a span-only method to elicit thought processes from models without corrupting those processes.

My rewrite and other comments sit, for days, now approaching weeks, unmoderated....

I make another short comment. Someone writes about how they built an automated research scaffold. I point out that maybe, alongside their scaffold, they might want to RL some models to specifically look for the most interesting stuff in the infinite stream of nonsense the scaffold produces. At this point I am annoyed and don’t really want to develop in long detail what the concept is, just give enough to say ‘hey, here is a direction you could take this research that might be interesting’.

I get a message, finally a human has moderated an actual comment!

Insufficient Quality for AI Content.

Well at least it isn’t a yellow fucking flag. 

I’m driven to drink. Only half of something called a Punch Romaine à la Carpathia on this godforsaken floating retirement home in the middle of the Caribbean that I’ve chained myself to in the attempt to have a good time before the end of the world. I look out at an ocean that seems to embody the sublime blue. Is my writing really that bad? Am I that incomprehensible? Why can’t my considerable poetic talent ever turn into publishable anything? 

There are other places I could publish, I think darkly. In fact I will, if it gets rejected here. But that won’t be sufficient to satisfy my frustration: my passion demands an œuvre...

Now my mind turns to petty revenge. I’ve been to LessOnline twice. I’ve drunk in the unspeakable beauty of Berkeley. I once kissed a boy at Lighthaven. I exist in the real world too, Goddamnit! I know what I can do: at the next LessOnline I can subject every moderator who rejected me to fifteen minutes of my possibly very annoying company, just long enough that politeness dictates that they actually have to bear annoyance IRL. Bwahahahaha!

Meh, that seems like a lot of effort. I’d probably rather spend my time eating canapés.

Or, if they had actually understood my Death and Immortality piece they would understand that we will all live a very long time. Thus, in the P(doom) scenarios we will not die but instead will have no mouth and yet feel the urge to scream. Perhaps the evil AI will torture them with a perpetual succession of individuals very much like me, but not exactly me, all of whom will annoy them for 15 minutes at a time in a simulated Lighthaven and ensure that they never again will kiss a boy. 

I have written it, so now it is possible and since it is possible, then by the power of the many-worlds interpretation there is a future where it will happen.

Just as, in some unhappy timeline, my personal AI demon will torture me perpetually with the phrase:

Too many yellow flags. 



Discuss
